intro: About one in four people on earth is Muslim, by common estimates close to two billion people, from Indonesia and Pakistan to Nigeria, Turkey and the neighborhoods of Chicago. Many of them begin each day with a prayer said before sunrise, facing a small stone building in a valley in western Arabia. This unit asks where that practice comes from and what it means to the people who keep it.

You will start in seventh-century Mecca and Medina, with the life of Muhammad as Muslims understand it and the book Muslims call the Qur'an, God's word recited in Arabic. You will study the Five Pillars that shape a Muslim's day, year and life. Then you will follow the tradition outward: the Prophet's example in the hadith, the law scholars built from it, the split between Sunni and Shia, the inner path of the Sufis, and a golden age of learning that stretched from Baghdad to Córdoba to Timbuktu.

By the end you will be able to explain the core beliefs and practices of Islam in its own terms, read a passage of the Qur'an or a hadith and say what its author and audience are doing, describe the diversity among Muslims without flattening it, and write about Islam the way a scholar of religion does: attributing each belief, comparing without ranking, and citing the sources.
bigQuestion: How do a book, a Prophet's example and five simple practices shape the lives of nearly two billion people, and why do Muslims live them out in so many different ways?

timeline.t: Muhammad is born in Mecca, according to Islamic tradition
Muslims believe the first verses of the Qur'an are revealed on Mount Hira
The hijra: Muhammad and his followers move to Medina; year 1 of the Islamic calendar
Muhammad dies in Medina; Abu Bakr becomes the first caliph
The Qur'an's text is fixed in official copies under the caliph Uthman
Husayn is killed at Karbala, the event Shia Muslims mourn on Ashura
The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founds Baghdad
Al-Khwarizmi writes his book on al-jabr, the source of the word algebra
Death of al-Bukhari, compiler of the most trusted Sunni hadith collection
Mansa Musa of Mali makes the hajj and brings scholars home to West Africa
The Nation of Islam is founded in Detroit; it is later led from Chicago

words.d: recitation; the scripture of Islam, which Muslims believe is God's word revealed to Muhammad in Arabic
the absolute oneness of God, the central belief of Islam
the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622, which begins the Islamic calendar
the five basic duties of Islam: shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj
ritual prayer performed five times a day facing Mecca
the pilgrimage to Mecca, required once in a lifetime for Muslims who are able
a report of what the Prophet Muhammad said, did or approved
the example of the Prophet, known through the hadith
the path of divine guidance for all of life that Muslims believe God has given
a successor who led the Muslim community after Muhammad, without prophetic authority
the mystical path within Islam, seeking direct, inward knowledge and love of God

test.q: What do Muslims believe happened on Mount Hira in about 610?
choices: Muhammad received the first revelation of the Qur'an through the angel Gabriel
Muhammad migrated to Medina
Abraham built the Kaaba
The first mosque was built
test.why: Islamic tradition holds that Gabriel brought the first verses, from Sura 96, to Muhammad in a cave on Mount Hira.

test.q: Why does the Islamic calendar count its years from 622 CE?
choices: It is the year of the Battle of Badr
It is the year of the hijra, the migration from Mecca to Medina
It is the year of Muhammad's birth
It is the year Baghdad was founded
test.why: The hijra to Medina marks year 1 of the Islamic calendar, abbreviated AH.

test.q: What does tawhid mean, and what is its opposite?
choices: Prayer; its opposite is fasting
Law; its opposite is custom
The oneness of God; its opposite is shirk, associating anything with God
Pilgrimage; its opposite is migration
test.why: Tawhid, God's absolute oneness, is the center of Islamic belief; shirk is its opposite and the gravest error.

test.q: Which list names the Five Pillars of Islam?
choices: Qur'an, hadith, ijma, qiyas and fatwa
Sunni, Shia, Sufi, Hanafi and Maliki
Tawhid, prophets, angels, scripture and judgment
Shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj
test.why: The pillars are the declaration of faith, prayer, required giving, the Ramadan fast and the pilgrimage.

test.q: Why do Muslims consider an English translation an interpretation rather than the Qur'an itself?
choices: They believe the Qur'an is God's speech in its revealed Arabic words
English translations were banned by the caliphs
The Qur'an was first written in Greek
Only scholars may read translations
test.why: Muslims hold the Arabic text to be God's own words, so any translation conveys only its meaning.

test.q: How does Ramadan's place in the solar year change?
choices: It stays in the same month every year
It moves about eleven days earlier each year because the Islamic calendar is lunar
It moves later each year because of leap years
It always falls in winter
test.why: The lunar year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan cycles through all the seasons.

test.q: Which pair of festivals is correctly described?
choices: Eid al-Fitr marks the hajj; Eid al-Adha ends Ramadan
Ashura ends Ramadan; Eid al-Fitr remembers Karbala
Eid al-Fitr ends the Ramadan fast; Eid al-Adha recalls Abraham's sacrifice during the hajj
Both Eids fall on fixed dates of the solar calendar
test.why: Eid al-Fitr breaks the fast of Ramadan; Eid al-Adha falls on the day of sacrifice during the hajj.

test.q: How does a hadith differ from a verse of the Qur'an, in Muslim understanding?
choices: A hadith is always longer
A hadith is written only in Persian
The Qur'an records the Prophet's deeds, while hadith record God's words
A hadith is a human report of the Prophet's words or deeds, while the Qur'an is believed to be God's word
test.why: Hadith are reports about Muhammad that scholars grade; the Qur'an is held to be God's revealed speech.

test.q: What does the word fiqh refer to?
choices: The human effort of scholars to understand and apply sharia
The pilgrimage to Karbala
The Sufi practice of remembrance
The niche in a mosque wall
test.why: Fiqh, or understanding, is jurisprudence: scholars' fallible work of applying the guidance Muslims call sharia.

test.q: Which statement about Sunni and Shia Muslims is accurate?
choices: Shia Muslims are the majority worldwide
They divided over who should lead after Muhammad, and they share the Qur'an and the Five Pillars
They use different Qur'ans
Sunnis reject the hajj
test.why: The division began over succession; both branches share the Qur'an, the pillars and the hajj.

test.q: Rumi and the Mevlevi order are most closely connected with which part of Islam?
choices: The Hanbali school of law
The Twelver Shia Imams
Sufism, the mystical inner path
The Abbasid translation movement
test.why: Rumi was a Sufi poet, and the Mevlevi order, known for its turning prayer, grew from his followers.

test.q: Which contribution is correctly matched with its scholar?
choices: Rumi: the Canon of Medicine
Ibn Sina: the first English translation of the Qur'an
Al-Bukhari: the first book of algebra
Al-Khwarizmi: a book on al-jabr that gave algebra its name
test.why: Al-Khwarizmi's book on al-jabr gave us algebra; Ibn Sina wrote the Canon, and al-Bukhari compiled hadith.

test.q: Why are there no images of God or people inside a mosque?
choices: Because of tawhid and the concern that images could lead to shirk
Because Muslims have no artistic tradition
Because mosques are always too small
Because each imam personally forbids decoration
test.why: Tawhid and the fear of shirk lead mosques to use calligraphy and pattern instead of images.

test.q: Which facts link Islam to Chicago's history?
choices: The Kaaba was first built in Chicago
Elijah Muhammad led the Nation of Islam from Chicago, and the city is home to many diverse mosques today
The House of Wisdom stood on Devon Avenue
Mansa Musa visited Chicago in 1324
test.why: The Nation of Islam was led from Chicago, and the region's Muslims today come from dozens of backgrounds.

test.q: A Muslim family in Illinois buys meat labeled zabiha. What does that label promise?
choices: The meat is vegetarian
The meat was shipped from Mecca
The animal was slaughtered in the prescribed Islamic way, with God's name spoken and the blood drained
The meat was blessed by a Sufi sheikh
test.why: Zabiha is the Islamic method of slaughter that makes permitted meat halal.

write.prompt: How does Islam balance firm rules with mercy and intention? Using two or three sources from this unit, such as Sura 2:185 on the fast, the hadith on intentions, and Rabi'a's prayer, explain what different Muslims, including jurists and Sufis, would say and why.
tips: Name each source you cite, with sura and verse or the hadith collection.
Attribute every belief: write Muslims believe, or many Sufis teach.
Show diversity among Muslims, such as different schools of law or Sunni and Shia views.
Compare and explain; do not judge whether a belief is true.
Use the unit's terms, such as sharia, fiqh, Sunnah and dhikr, and define them.
